genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a technician looks after an optical instrument set up at high elevation
she does her work through the night
the site was picked far from town lighting
grime on the mirror blunted the sharpness of the images
washing it often would have harmed the reflecting surface
with a mechanic she designed a movable cover that the wind sets off
the arrangement kept the quality of the observations intact
a second one is planned for the instrument alongside
text: You could pass her in a hallway and never guess she spends her nights minding a telescope. It sits high on a windy plateau, well away from the glow of any town, which was the whole point of putting it up there. Dust was her headache, she says. Within a week the mirror would go gray and the pictures lost their edge. Washing it often would have worn the reflecting coat right off, so she went looking for another way. Working with a mechanic, she rigged a soft cover that swings shut the moment the wind picks up. The mirror has stayed bright ever since, and the frames come out crisp. She laughs it off, as though anyone would have hit on the same trick. Her coworkers know better: that cover has saved whole nights of work. She is building a second one now for the instrument next door.

units: two sky projection halls have opened in the same region
the first one banks on visual intensity
that intensity wears the viewer out instead of teaching him
the second hall takes a plainer approach
its spoken narration lays out how orbits work
the stretch given over to comets exposes the gap between the two
admission prices are much the same
the writer plainly recommends the second hall
the second hall also runs a showing with no spoken narration
text: Two sky theaters have opened in the same region, and the comparison lands squarely in favor of the second. The first one banks everything on force. Its dome buries you under a torrent of stars so fierce that it dazzles far more than it teaches, and you come out dizzy with nothing held in your head. The second holds back. Its darker vault gives the eye room to breathe, and a spoken narration walks you through the workings of an orbit instead of decorating it. The gap shows plainly in the comet stretch: where one piles on effects, the other simply follows an icy core warming as it draws near its star. Admission runs to much the same either way. The second house also offers a showing with no narration at all, given over to silence. That choice, at any rate, is anything but silent.

units: the narrator writes from a terrace she used to visit with the woman she is writing to
she holds on to three sights from the evening
the color of dusk fades away behind a ridge
a satellite crosses the sky without a sound
the pale trail of our galaxy strikes her as beyond describing
she has kept a star chart given to her long ago
that chart helps her find again the star figures she was taught
she asks the woman she is writing to to come back
she spoke out loud to her absent friend
text: I am writing from the terrace we used to climb to, and the sky above it is every bit as wide as you remember. Three sights stayed with me tonight. First the color of dusk, going violet before it drained away behind the ridge. Then a satellite, a patient point of light sliding across the vault without a sound. And last the silver dust of our galaxy, which I have never managed to describe without spoiling its softness. I brought along your old star chart, the one worn transparent at the folds. It still helps me pick out the figures you taught me. Warm wind carried the smell of dry grass, and I caught myself talking to you out loud. Nothing up there has changed, and that comforts me more than I had expected it would. Come back whenever you like. The terrace is waiting, and so am I.

units: liftoff starts once the thrust outweighs the whole assembly
the opening phase serves to get through the dense layers of air
the lower stage lets go once its propellant is used up
that stage falls into a sea area chosen in advance
the launcher then tips its path over
that tipping supplies the sideways speed an orbit calls for
the nose shroud opens when air friction no longer counts
the payload lets go and makes contact with a station on the ground
the phases are set off by physical thresholds and not by a clock
text: People often ask what goes on in the half hour after a launch, and the answer is a strict run of steps. The vehicle leaves the pad the instant its thrust outweighs the whole assembly, and those first seconds are spent punching up through the dense lower air in a blaze of flame. Next the bottom stage, its propellant spent, lets go. Where does it end up? In a stretch of open sea picked out well beforehand. Does the rocket turn at that point? It does. It tips its climb over to build sideways speed, because an orbit is held by speed rather than by height. The nose shroud splits open once air friction stops counting. The payload releases at last, and its antenna reaches for the station that will track it from the ground. Every step fires on a measured threshold, never on a clock set beforehand.

units: the operations manager announces that a maneuver is put off
a flare on the nearby star has loaded the upper air with particles
that load disturbs the radio links
an engineer asks whether the docking can happen all the same
the manager says no and gives his grounds for it
without a steady link the automatic pilot stops receiving its corrections
a crew member points out that the water reserves are ample
the maneuver will start again once the stream of particles has eased
text: The operations manager informed the crew that the maneuver would have to be put off. A flare on the nearest star, he explained, had loaded the upper air with charged particles, and the radio links were suffering badly for it. The flight engineer asked whether the craft might dock all the same before the rotation ended. He answered that it could not, and he gave his grounds: with no steady link, the automatic pilot would stop receiving its corrections, and the approach would turn hazardous for everyone aboard. One member of the crew observed that the water reserves on board were ample. The manager closed the exchange by saying that waiting would therefore cost nothing beyond a measure of patience, and that the maneuver would start again as soon as the stream of particles had eased.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: angle measurements disagreed from one observer to another
wooden instruments warped under damp air
the unaided eye held back how fine the readings could be
metal took the place of wood for the sake of steadiness
adding a telescope to the moving arm cut the error to a tenth
people grasped that the date and the warmth of the air had to be written down
those notes served to allow afterward for swelling and shrinking
sky watching became in this way a strict craft of measurement
observing notebooks survive and bear out this practice
text: Early sky watchers ran into a stubborn trouble: the angles they measured never quite agreed from one observer to the next, and nobody could settle who was right. Wooden instruments warped as damp air soaked into them, and the unaided eye could fix a position only so finely and no further. The remedy came in stages. Metal took the place of wood, being far steadier under weather. A small telescope was then mounted on the moving arm, which cut the error to a tenth of what it had been. Last came the grasp that every sighting had to be written down with its date and the warmth of the air, so that swelling and shrinking could be allowed for afterward. That habit of writing changed the trade: sky watching stopped being a gift of keen eyesight and became a craft of measurement. The surviving notebooks show it, page after cramped page.

units: an asteroid is a dry heavy block
it has circled close to its star since the system took shape
its shape shifts little despite rounds of heating and cooling
a comet comes from the far cold reaches
it mixes ice with rocky rubble
as it nears the star its ice turns straight into gas
that change draws out a long tail
both bodies bear witness to the same old beginning
the tail points away from the star whatever the direction of travel
text: Want to get the difference between an asteroid and a comet? Picture two stones. The first is dry, heavy and dusty, and it has been circling close to the star ever since the system took shape. Heat it, cool it, heat it again, and it hardly alters. The second one comes from much farther out, from the black cold at the edge. Ice is packed into it along with grit and rubble. Out there it looks much like the first. But let it swing in close and the ice turns straight to gas, drawing behind it a tail that stretches an enormous way. There is the whole difference: one is a leftover rock, the other a frozen lump that shows what it is by melting. One more thing worth knowing. That tail always points away from the star, whichever way the body happens to be traveling. Both carry the same old beginning, but only the second puts on a show.

units: a power cut left a neighborhood without lighting
neighbors who never spoke sat down together to watch the sky
a retired teacher set his telescope up on a roof
he showed the rings of a planet to children
a cashier photographed the night sky with her phone
her picture showed a blurred but recognizable streak
the power came back at sunrise
a good many of those there were sorry to see it return
the company running the grid blames a faulty transformer
text: The power cut that dropped a whole neighborhood into darkness turned out to have an odd upside. Three scenes tell it. In one courtyard, neighbors who had never so much as traded a word ended up sitting side by side, heads tipped back, counting the stars that had come out all at once. On a nearby roof, a retired teacher hauled out his telescope and put on a show on the spot, holding the rings of a pale planet steady for children who had never seen anything of the kind. Outside a darkened movie house, a cashier aimed her phone at the sky and got, to her own surprise, a blurred streak that anyone could still recognize. The power came back at sunrise. Plenty of those out that night owned up to being almost sorry it had. The company running the grid points to a fault in a transformer.

units: you have to pick a night with no moonlight in it
the eyes need a long spell of getting used to the dark
the watcher lies down on a blanket before sweeping his eyes across the sky
he follows a shape he has spotted until he ties it to a figure he knows
the star chart comes out only after that step
a red filter guards night sight
a falling star may show up toward the east late in the watch
the gear is packed away before the damp gets at it
it is worth writing down what you saw before going to sleep
text: Pick a night with no moon in it, and a rise of ground where your eye can run free. Give your eyes their long slow surrender to the dark, since faint stars will not show themselves to anybody in a hurry. Spread a blanket, lie back, and let your gaze wander the vault without trying yet to name a single thing. When some shape stands out, follow it until it settles into a figure you know. Only then bring out your chart, under a red filter that spares your night sight. Compare, doubt, begin again. Toward the end of your watch, turn to the east, where now and then a falling star cuts across and burns out in a short bright line. Write down what you saw before you sleep, or the next night will blur it. Pack your gear away before the damp works its way into it, and go back down slowly.

units: the count of satellites in low orbit is climbing steeply
each satellite throws the light of the central star back toward the ground
its passage across a sensor leaves a bright mark on the exposure
that mark floods the sensitive elements it touches
faint bodies sitting behind it become impossible to pick up
teams have to throw the frame out or rebuild it by computation
one observatory found that one exposure in ten was hit early in the night
the builders are darkening the surfaces that catch the light
the first trials halve the glare thrown back
text: The swelling crowd of satellites in low orbit now weighs on astronomical work, and the mechanism behind it is well understood. Each craft throws the light of the central star back down toward the ground, and when one crosses a sensor during a long exposure, it writes a bright streak across the frame. That streak floods the sensitive elements it touches, so that faint bodies sitting behind it drop out of reach altogether. Teams are left with two costly ways out: throw the frame away, or rebuild the ruined strip by computation. One observatory found that one exposure in ten was spoiled in the early part of the night. The builders have answered by darkening the surfaces that catch the light, and the first trials halve the glare thrown back. For wide field instruments the trouble is as sharp as ever.
